title: Upper Limb Anatomy
subject: Anatomy
summary: The upper limb includes the shoulder girdle, arm, forearm and hand, supplied by the brachial plexus and major vessels. Understanding its layout guides diagnosis of trauma, neurovascular injury and common tropical conditions.

sections.p: The upper limb enables manipulation, posture and locomotion of the hand. It is organized into proximal (shoulder girdle, arm) and distal (forearm, hand) units, each with distinct neurovascular patterns.
b: Four regions: shoulder girdle, arm, forearm, hand
Key bones: scapula, clavicle, humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges
Clinical relevance: injuries often involve multiple structures simultaneously

sections.p: The shoulder girdle (clavicle and scapula) anchors the limb to the trunk. The humerus forms the arm; the radius and ulna form the forearm; the hand consists of 27 bones.
b: Glenoid fossa articulates with humeral head (ball‑and‑socket)
Elbow joint: humeroulnar (hinge) and radioulnar (pivot)
Carpometacarpal joint of thumb allows opposition

sections.p: Muscles, vessels and nerves lie in defined compartments. The axilla houses the brachial plexus, axillary artery and lymph nodes, while the forearm compartments separate flexors (anterior) from extensors (posterior).
b: Anterior compartment: flexor digitorum superficialis, median nerve
Posterior compartment: extensor carpi radialis, radial nerve
First dorsal interosseous lies between metacarpals 1 and 2

sections.p: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib, then the brachial artery down the arm, dividing into radial and ulnar arteries at the elbow.
b: Axillary artery: 1st, 2nd, 3rd parts give off thoraco‑acromial, lateral thoracic, subscapular, posterior circumflex humeral arteries
Brachial artery: profunda brachii supplies posterior arm
Radial artery: supplies lateral forearm and hand; ulnar artery supplies medial hand

sections.p: The brachial plexus (C5‑T1) forms five major trunks that give rise to the major peripheral nerves of the limb: musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar.
b: Musculocutaneous: flexes elbow, sensory to lateral forearm
Axillary: deltoid and teres minor motor, lateral shoulder sensation
Radial: wrist/ finger extension, dorsal hand sensation
Median: thenar muscles, flexion of wrist and fingers, palmar thumb‑side sensation
Ulnar: intrinsic hand muscles, medial hand sensation

sections.p: The upper limb provides gross power (shoulder, elbow) and fine dexterity (wrist, hand). Coordination of agonist‑antagonist pairs and proprioceptive feedback from muscle spindles and joint receptors allow precise movements.
b: Shoulder abduction (deltoid) vs adduction (pectoralis major)
Elbow flexion (biceps) vs extension (triceps)
Wrist flexion (flexor carpi radialis) vs extension (extensor carpi ulnaris)
Finger opposition (thenar muscles) enables grasp

sections.p: Trauma, infections and tropical diseases often present with neurovascular compromise. Recognising patterns of loss helps localise lesions and plan urgent care.
b: Fracture of surgical neck of humerus → axillary nerve palsy (deltoid weakness, loss of lateral shoulder sensation)
Mid‑shaft humeral fracture → radial nerve injury (wrist drop, loss of sensation over dorsum of hand)
Forearm compartment syndrome (often after crush injury or severe malaria) → pain out of proportion, tense compartments, loss of distal pulses; urgent fasciotomy needed
Tuberculous osteomyelitis of the humerus (common in low‑resource settings) → chronic pain, swelling, sinus formation
Herbal poultice‑induced cellulitis → rapid swelling, erythema, systemic signs; consider Staphylococcus aureus or atypical mycobacteria

sections.p: A systematic bedside exam starts proximally and proceeds distally, integrating motor, sensory and vascular checks.
b: Inspect for deformity, swelling, skin changes
Palpate bony landmarks (acromion, humeral epicondyles) for tenderness
Assess shoulder range (abduction, external rotation) – deltoid and rotator cuff function
Test elbow flexion/extension – biceps/triceps strength
Wrist and finger movements – radial, median, ulnar nerve integrity
Sensory testing: pinprick over lateral forearm (musculocutaneous), dorsum of hand (radial), palmar thumb side (median), medial hand (ulnar)
Vascular: radial pulse, capillary refill, compare bilateral blood pressure

t.b: Is arterial flow to the hand adequate? Absence suggests brachial or radial artery injury; if unavailable, assess capillary refill and skin colour
Is there upper motor neuron involvement? Positive sign suggests cervical cord compression or central lesion
Does the forearm have compartment syndrome? Pressure >30 mmHg warrants fasciotomy; if a manometer is unavailable, rely on clinical signs (pain, tense swelling, loss of pulses)

whenToSeekHelp: Absent radial pulse with expanding forearm swelling
Progressive neurological deficit (e.g., worsening hand weakness) after trauma
Signs of systemic infection (fever, tachycardia) with a limb wound

faq.q: Why does a mid‑shaft humeral fracture often cause wrist drop?
faq.a: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humerus; fracture can damage it, leading to loss of wrist and finger extension.

faq.q: What is the first step in suspected compartment syndrome of the forearm?
faq.a: Remove any constrictive dressings and assess pain with passive stretch; if severe, arrange urgent fasciotomy.

faq.q: How can you differentiate axillary nerve injury from deltoid muscle tear?
faq.a: Axillary nerve injury causes loss of sensation over the lateral shoulder and inability to abduct beyond 15°, while a pure muscle tear may retain sensation.

exam: A patient presents with a fractured surgical neck of humerus; which nerve is most likely injured and what clinical signs confirm it? — Look for deltoid weakness and loss of lateral shoulder sensation (axillary nerve).

During a malaria epidemic, a child develops painful swelling of the forearm after a fall; what emergency diagnosis must you consider and how do you confirm it without a pressure monitor? — Forearm compartment syndrome; diagnose by tense swelling, pain on passive stretch, and loss of distal pulses.

A farmer with chronic cough and weight loss has a painless swelling over the proximal humerus; what tropical infection should be high on your list and what investigation is essential? — Tuberculous osteomyelitis; obtain X‑ray and, if possible, a GeneXpert or acid‑fast smear of aspirate.

You examine a patient with wrist drop; the radial pulse is present. Which level of nerve injury is most likely and why? — Injury to the radial nerve distal to the brachial artery, often at the spiral groove, sparing vascular supply.

A patient with sickle cell disease presents with sudden hand pain and swelling; what vaso‑occlusive complication should you suspect and what immediate management is required? — Hand‑foot syndrome (dactylitis); give analgesia, hydration, and consider exchange transfusion if severe.

During a routine exam you find a positive Hoffmann’s sign in a 45‑year‑old with neck pain; what central lesion does this suggest and what imaging is indicated? — Cervical cord compression; order MRI of the cervical spine.

A child with a deep laceration on the forearm is brought from a rural clinic lacking cultures; what empirical antibiotics cover common pathogens and why avoid aminoglycosides? — Use a first‑generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefazolin) for Staphylococcus; avoid aminoglycosides due to nephrotoxicity and limited efficacy against gram‑positive skin flora.

In a patient with a humeral fracture, you note loss of sensation over the medial hand; which nerve is injured and what functional deficit will develop? — Ulnar nerve injury; loss of intrinsic hand muscle function leading to claw hand.
